Waddah lived in a village on a mountain. Its fields were like steps, one above the other. And he loved to hear people say, "How generous Waddah is!"

Whenever his father picked the grapes, Waddah carried a basket to the masjid courtyard after the prayer, where the men sat, and called out loudly, "Help yourselves! These grapes are from our house!"

One day his sister Arwa gave him a basket and said, "Take it to Uncle Mutahhar. He is a very old man who cannot see, and he never leaves his house."

Uncle Mutahhar's house was at the far end of the village, on a path where nobody ever walked. Waddah looked at the empty path, then he looked at the courtyard.

So he walked to the courtyard and handed out the grapes to the men until the basket was empty. They said, "May Allah bless you, Waddah! How generous you are!"

He went home happy, and he did not tell Arwa where he had taken the basket.

In the evening he sat with the boys by the well and told them what the men had said. Then he told it again to those who came after them, and then to everyone he met on the way.

His friend Nashwan listened and said nothing. In his hand was an empty jar.

On the way to the fields there was a big smooth rock. The wind had gathered a little soil on top of it, and green grass had grown in it.

Waddah said to Nashwan, "Look! The rock is greener than your father's field!" Nashwan said, "Its green is on top of stone. It has no roots to hold it."

Early in the morning, Waddah saw Nashwan climbing the empty path with a jar of water to Uncle Mutahhar's house, so he followed him.

He said, "Why tire yourself out here? Nobody can see you!" Nashwan said, "Uncle Mutahhar gets to drink, and Allah sees me. Isn't that enough?"

That night heavy rain fell, and Waddah heard the water running down the mountain until morning.

When the sun came up, he went out with Nashwan and Arwa. They passed the rock — and it was smooth and clean, with no soil on it and not a single blade of grass. But the fields below it were greener than before.

Arwa said, "In Surat Al-Baqarah there is a parable about someone who gives his wealth so that people will see him." Then she recited:

﴿فَمَثَلُهُ كَمَثَلِ صَفْوَانٍ عَلَيْهِ تُرَابٌ فَأَصَابَهُ وَابِلٌ فَتَرَكَهُ صَلْدًا﴾

She said, "Safwan is a smooth stone, wabil is very heavy rain, and sald is something smooth with nothing left on it."

Waddah stood in front of the rock for a long time. He remembered the men in the courtyard, then he said, "My grapes were soil on a stone."

Nashwan said, "And the rain did not take away the soil of the fields, because it is deep and the roots hold it. And Uncle Mutahhar is still waiting for his grapes."

In the afternoon Waddah carried a basket along the empty path. He sat with Uncle Mutahhar and handed him the grapes one by one, and the old man prayed for him.

When he came back, the boys by the well asked him, "Where were you?" He almost told them, then he said, "I had something to do." And in his heart was a joy he had never known before.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever does good deeds so that people will hear about them, Allah will let people hear what he really intended; and whoever does good deeds to be seen, Allah will show people what he really is."

📖 Agreed upon (Al-Bukhari and Muslim). This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.
note:
**The meaning of the hadith**
Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has made the reward match the deed. Whoever is sincere in his deed and intends by it the Face of Allah will have the fullest reward. And whoever acts with a different intention, Allah, glorified is He, deals with him in a way that goes against what he aimed for and contradicts his intention in that deed, so that he may be deterred within himself.

In this hadith the Prophet ﷺ says: "Whoever makes things heard, Allah will make him heard," meaning: whoever announces people's faults and disgraces them, and does not cover them as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded him, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will disgrace him and remove his cover in this world and on the Day of Resurrection before all creation, and will bring out what he used to hide from them. The same applies to whoever seeks praise and admiration from people through his deeds, and seeks reputation and fame among people for something.

"And whoever shows off" — seeking by his deed something other than sincerity, so that people will talk about him, out of a wish for praise and admiration. Showing off (riya') is abandoning sincerity in words and deeds: saying something or doing something without wanting by it the Face of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. "Allah will show him off" means that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, makes the reward and the deed of the show-off belong to the people, and does not reward him for it; for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, accepts no deed except one done purely for His Noble Face.

📖 From the Hadith Encyclopedia — Dorar.net.

**Talk with your child**
1. Why did Waddah go to the courtyard, and not to Uncle Mutahhar's house?
2. What was left for Waddah of the men's praise a day later? And what was left for Nashwan?
3. Is all giving in front of people showing off? (No, what counts is the intention: ﴿إِن تُبْدُوا الصَّدَقَاتِ فَنِعِمَّا هِيَ﴾ (If you give charity openly, how good that is!). Showing off is when people's praise is the aim.)

**This week's exercise**
Every day your child does a small good deed in secret and tells no one about it. At the end of the week, they tell you how they felt, without saying what they did.
